problem: Gaussian-splatting panoptic/open-vocabulary segmentation methods must accumulate high-channel feature vectors from all overlapping Gaussians per pixel, which makes rendering too slow for robotic control loops. Existing GS accelerations target RGB/depth and 3DGS, not 2DGS high-channel feature rendering.
motivation: Real-time segmentation rendering is needed as a sensor simulator and as a source of 3D-consistent multi-view labels for training robot perception. NeRF is slow, and prior GS panoptic methods (e.g. PanopticSplatting) are either multi-stage or slow.
key_idea: Build an end-to-end 2DGS panoptic reconstruction with query-guided instance features, and speed up inference by Precise Tile Intersection (Snugbox/AccuTile for surfels) and Top-K Hard Selection, which accumulates features only from the top-K Gaussians per pixel.
insight: 2DGS surfels are thin and geometrically sparse, so only a few front-most primitives are needed to render segmentation features. In the ablation, Top-K cuts rendered Gaussians from 6.1M to 1.2M and time from 46 to 27 ms while PQ moves only from 74.75 to 74.17. Precise Tile Intersection removes redundant tile assignments (6.1M to 3.9M) at almost no PQ cost.
method: Base representation: 2D Gaussian surfels (LI-GS base), with 16-d semantic features and 32-d instance features per Gaussian, supervised by Grounded-SAM 2D masks

Query-guided instance segmentation: learnable Gaussian instance queries; affinity = sigmoid(f_q^T f_ins) times a density-ratio spatial proximity weight; softmax over queries, alpha-blended into pixel labels

Instance query alignment: per-frame Hungarian matching between rendered and pseudo-GT binary masks, with Dice+BCE instance loss, CE semantic loss, L1+SSIM RGB loss, and depth/SDF/eikonal/panoptic terms
Precise Tile Intersection: perspective-corrected conic (inverse projected covariance) fed to AccuTile for exact tile extent and Snugbox for tight traversal, reducing tile-to-surfel assignments
Top-K Hard Selection: at inference, feature accumulation is restricted to the K=24 most contributory Gaussians per pixel, ordered by visibility and depth
Applications: render RGB/depth/panoptic from Gazebo camera poses as a sensor simulator; use 3D-consistent 2D boxes as labels to fine-tune the closed-set detector in VLFM-based ObjectNav

setting.backbone: 2D Gaussian Splatting (LI-GS base) with instance queries, per-scene optimized; Grounded-SAM (frozen) for 2D supervision; YOLOv13 detector fine-tuned in the nav use case
setting.training_data: Per-scene optimization on multi-view RGB-D from 4 ScanNet-V2 scenes and 3 ScanNet++ scenes, plus 10 real-world indoor scenes (RGB + LiDAR) for navigation; the detector is fine-tuned on labels generated from the reconstructions
setting.observation: multi-view RGB-D frames (posed) for reconstruction; RGB-D observations for the VLFM navigation agent
setting.action_space: VLFM frontier-based ObjectNav decisions; Jackal UGV commands in Gazebo
setting.simulator: Gazebo (with meshes from ScanNet++); reconstructed real-world scenes for navigation
setting.privileged: Scene reconstruction from pre-captured RGB-D of the test environments, used to generate fine-tuning labels (test scenes are seen during label generation)

numbers_note: The paper's only navigation results are the custom object-goal tables on 10 private real-world scenes (SR before/after fine-tuning: Laboratory Room 20% to 100%, House 25% to 50%). These are not on a canonical benchmark, so they are not listed as benchmark rows. The panoptic segmentation and speed results are also outside the canonical benchmark list.
results: On ScanNet, Fast-SegSim reaches PQ 74.12 and mIoU 74.93, versus PanopticRecon at PQ 63.70 and mIoU 68.62. On ScanNet++ it reaches PQ 77.09, versus Panoptic Lifting at 71.14. The full pipeline renders in 22 ms (45 FPS) versus 46 ms (22 FPS) for the baseline, and fine-tuning the detector with its labels raises ObjectNav SR from 20% to 100% (lab) and 25% to 50% (house).
limitations: Navigation evaluation is tiny and non-standard: two scenes, apparently few episodes, no public benchmark, and test scenes are the same ones the labels were generated from.

The Top-K selection is a heuristic with fixed K=24, evaluated only on a few scenes with PQ as the sole quality check; the 50+ FPS claim in the abstract is not matched by the 45 FPS in the ablation and conclusion.
The Gazebo real-time simulation demonstration is qualitative only, and no real robot experiments are reported.
